title: Understanding the Layers of an Agentic AI System
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to distinguish workflows from agents and analyze an agentic AI system as interacting reasoning, capability, coordination, and assurance layers. After completing it, learners can identify each layer's responsibility and diagnose where a described behavior originates.
objectives: Distinguish a workflow with predefined execution paths from an agent that dynamically directs its own process.
Classify system components into reasoning, capability, coordination, and assurance layers.
Trace a task through the layers and identify which layer is responsible for a failure or decision.
Explain why evaluation and risk management apply to the complete system rather than only to its language model.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you understand basic language-model concepts such as prompts and generated responses. It does not assume experience with a particular provider, programming interface, or configuration system.

The four-layer model used here is a teaching framework, not a claim that every source or system uses standardized layer names. It separates responsibilities so that a learner can inspect how an agentic system reasons, obtains capabilities, coordinates work, and manages risk.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous source record, content/modules/agentic-ai-literacy/agentic-ai-layers.json, was a repository-local path attributed to an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. It was not an independently accessible supporting source.

That source record was replaced with directly accessible sources from Anthropic, arXiv, and the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology. The correction affects the module's source provenance, the distinction between workflows and agents, the description of interleaved reasoning and action, and the treatment of system-level risk management.
sections.callout: This update does not treat the former repository path as evidence for any factual claim.

sections.title: First identify the coordination pattern
paragraphs: A workflow and an agent can both combine a language model with external capabilities, but they coordinate work differently. In a workflow, predefined code paths determine the sequence or routing of operations. In an agent, the model dynamically directs its process and decides how to proceed.

This distinction concerns control, not the number of steps. A long predefined sequence is still a workflow. A system becomes agentic in this sense when the model has responsibility for choosing subsequent actions or directing how the task will be completed.

Before analyzing layers, ask who selects the next step. If a fixed path selects it, classify the coordination as a workflow. If the model selects it from available actions while pursuing a goal, classify it as agent-directed coordination.

sections.title: Reasoning layer
paragraphs: The reasoning layer interprets the current task and available information, then produces a proposed response, decision, or next action. In an agent-directed system, it may also revise its approach after receiving the result of an earlier action.

The ReAct paper demonstrates a method that interleaves reasoning traces with actions. Actions obtain new information from an external environment, and that information can inform later reasoning. The important architectural lesson is that reasoning and acting can form a repeated loop rather than a single prompt followed by a final response.

A reasoning failure occurs when the system has adequate information and capability but chooses an unsuitable conclusion or next step. That differs from a capability failure, in which the required information or action was unavailable.

sections.title: Capability layer
paragraphs: The capability layer supplies information or actions beyond what the reasoning component can produce by itself. The cited Anthropic source describes an augmented language model as one enhanced with capabilities such as retrieval, tools, and memory.

Retrieval can provide task-relevant information. A tool can perform an external operation or obtain an observation. Memory can preserve information that the system is designed to reuse. These are capability categories, not requirements that every system must implement.

A capability does not decide when it should be used. In a predefined workflow, code makes that decision. In an agent-directed arrangement, the reasoning and coordination process selects among available actions. Keeping this distinction clear helps determine whether a problem arose from an unavailable capability or from an incorrect decision to use it.

sections.title: Coordination layer
paragraphs: The coordination layer determines how work moves among reasoning steps and capabilities. It defines whether operations follow a fixed sequence, branch according to predefined rules, run in parallel, or are selected dynamically by an agent.

The cited Anthropic source presents prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker arrangements, and evaluator-optimizer arrangements as composable patterns. These patterns differ in how they divide work and choose subsequent steps.

To analyze coordination, trace one task from its initial request to completion. Record which component chooses each next step, what information that choice uses, and what result returns to the process. This trace reveals whether control is predefined, model-directed, or a combination of both.

sections.title: Assurance layer
paragraphs: The assurance layer covers the controls and evaluation practices used to identify and manage system risk. It surrounds the other layers because harmful or unreliable behavior can result from reasoning, capabilities, coordination, or their interaction.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework organizes risk-management work into the functions Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Applied as an analysis lens, these functions prompt teams to establish responsibilities, understand the operating context, assess behavior, and respond to identified risks.

Evaluation should therefore examine complete task traces and outcomes, not only isolated model responses. For example, a plausible reasoning step can still lead to an unacceptable outcome if coordination invokes an unsuitable capability. Conversely, a capability can operate correctly while the reasoning layer misinterprets its result.

sections.title: Diagnosing a layered system
paragraphs: Begin by describing the intended outcome. Then identify the reasoning component, the information and actions available through the capability layer, the mechanism that selects each next step, and the assurance measures applied to the resulting behavior.

Suppose a system receives sufficient information but selects an irrelevant action. Inspect reasoning and coordination. Suppose the selected action is appropriate but cannot obtain required information. Inspect the capability layer. Suppose all operational steps complete but an unacceptable outcome is neither detected nor handled. Inspect the assurance layer.

Layer boundaries are analytical rather than absolute. One implementation component may serve more than one responsibility. The purpose of the framework is to make responsibilities and failure locations explicit, not to require a particular implementation.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes an agent from a workflow in this module?
choices: An agent always performs more steps.
An agent dynamically directs its process, while a workflow follows predefined execution paths.
An agent cannot use external capabilities.
A workflow must produce only one response.
questions.explanation: The module defines the distinction in terms of control. Workflows use predefined paths, while agents dynamically direct how they proceed.

questions.prompt: A required source of information is unavailable to the system. Which layer should be inspected first?
questions.explanation: The capability layer provides external information and actions. Missing access to required information is therefore a capability issue.

questions.prompt: What question most directly reveals whether coordination is predefined or agent-directed?
choices: How many words are in the final response?
Who or what selects the next step?
How long is the initial request?
How many learners use the system?
questions.explanation: Tracing who or what selects each next step reveals whether control follows a fixed path or is directed dynamically by the model.

questions.prompt: Why does the assurance layer examine complete task traces rather than only isolated model responses?
choices: Because only coordination can create risk.
Because reasoning, capabilities, coordination, and their interactions can all contribute to an outcome.
Because model responses contain no useful information.
Because every system must use the same implementation.
questions.explanation: The module explains that unacceptable outcomes can arise from any layer or from interactions among layers, so assurance must consider the complete system behavior.
